title: Speed lives in memory, not the CPU
subtitle: A modern CPU is starving — fast code is mostly about feeding it well
concept:
Here is the surprise that reframes everything about performance: your CPU is almost never the bottleneck. A modern core can do a few simple arithmetic operations — add, multiply, compare — in well under a nanosecond. But when it needs a value that isn't already close by, it has to *wait*. Reaching into main memory costs on the order of 100 nanoseconds. In the time it takes to fetch one number from RAM, the CPU could have done a couple hundred adds. So the core spends most of its life idle, tapping its foot, waiting for data to show up. Speed isn't about making the CPU compute harder. It's about never letting it starve.

The fix is the *memory hierarchy*: small, blazing-fast caches sitting between the core and RAM. Data the CPU touched recently — or data sitting right next to data it touched — lives in cache, a few nanoseconds away instead of a hundred. The hardware is also a gambler: it watches your access pattern and *prefetches*, pulling in the next chunk before you ask, betting you'll walk memory in a straight line. So the recipe for fast code falls out almost by itself: keep the data small, keep it contiguous, and walk it in order. Do that and the CPU is fed a tight, predictable stream and rarely waits.

The simplest program that gets this exactly right is a *reduction*: sweep across one array, fold every element into a single running total. Summing an array — a checksum — is the canonical example. You touch each number exactly once, in order, and carry one accumulator in a register. Nothing is created, nothing is copied, nothing is thrown away. The prefetcher nails every guess. This is the floor of high performance, and it's worth internalizing before anything fancier: a tight loop over contiguous data with a running total in a register is about as fast as a computer goes.

And notice what this loop *doesn't* do — it never asks the system for memory. The array already exists; the total is one integer in a register. Zero heap allocations. That matters because allocation is the quiet opposite of everything above: it hands you fresh, cold, scattered memory the prefetcher has never seen, and later someone has to clean it up. The fast loop earns its speed partly by allocating nothing at all.
keyTakeaways: A CPU op is sub-nanosecond; a trip to main memory is ~100 ns. The core spends most of its time waiting on memory, not computing.
Caches + the hardware prefetcher reward small, contiguous, in-order data. Fast code feeds the CPU a predictable stream so it rarely stalls.
A reduction (sum/checksum) is the simplest fast loop: touch each element once, in order, carry one accumulator. Zero allocation.
Measured: post-SIMD N# sums 4096 i32 in 222.5 ns vs C#'s 994.7 ns — 4.5x faster than C#, ~2x behind native Rust/C (Apple M4, measured 2026-06).

nsharp.note: [hot] forbids allocation (NSYS010 would flag any); the compiler recognizes the reduction shape and emits SIMD, summing several lanes per step.

csharp.note: The honest C# baseline: zero allocations, but RyuJIT emits a scalar add per element, so it runs ~4.5x slower than the vectorized N# version.

rust.note: LLVM both vectorizes and unrolls the slice walk, which is why native still edges ahead — the gap is codegen quality, not the algorithm.

memoryStory: All three versions here allocate zero bytes on the heap — the array already exists and the total is one register — so this kernel is not where N# wins on memory (it doesn't differ). The real lesson is the cost model: a naive high-level version (C# `data.Where(...).Select(...).Sum()`, or building an intermediate `List<int>`) allocates per element or per stage, while the `[hot]` span loop allocates nothing and the NSYS010 analyzer *proves* it at build time. Zero is the measured number for this loop; the per-element allocation of the naive alternative is the illustrative contrast.

puzzle.prompt: Finish the `Checksum` reduction so it adds up every number in the array into a single running total, then print the total. This is the simplest fast loop there is: touch each element once, carry one accumulator, allocate nothing. The total of [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60] should come out to a whole number.
puzzle.successMessage: That's the floor of high performance: one in-order pass, one accumulator in a register, zero allocations. Everything faster is just feeding the CPU even better.
puzzle.hint: Inside the loop, add the current `number` to `total`. You can write it as `total = total + number` or `total += number` — both carry the running sum across iterations.

title: The heap and the stack: the silent allocation tax
subtitle: Why your tidy one-liner quietly mails an object to the garbage collector every call.
concept:
Your program keeps its data in two very different places. The **stack** is a scratchpad that grows and shrinks as functions call and return — every local `int`, every loop counter, every `span` view lives here. Putting a value on the stack is essentially free: the CPU just bumps a pointer, and when the function returns the whole frame vanishes at once. Nobody has to clean up. The **heap** is the opposite: a big shared pool of memory where long-lived or variably-sized objects live. Every time you write `new` on an array, a `List`, or a closure, the runtime carves out a chunk of the heap and hands you a reference to it.

The catch is that the heap has a janitor: the **garbage collector** (GC). The CPU spent cycles to allocate that object, and later the GC must spend more cycles walking memory to discover the object is dead and reclaim it. None of that work shows up in your source code — it's a *tax* charged on the side. One allocation is nothing. But the deadliest perf bug in managed code is a *hidden* allocation sitting inside a hot loop, paying that tax millions of times.

The trap is that the allocation is usually invisible. `numbers.Where(x => x > 0).Select(x => x * 2).ToList()` reads like a sentence, but each call allocates: the `Where` iterator is an object, the `Select` iterator is an object, the lambdas may capture into a closure object, and `ToList` grows a fresh backing array. You wrote one expressive line; you mailed five-plus objects to the GC. The fix is almost always the same shape: **don't build the intermediate collection at all.** Fuse the transform and the reduction into a single pass that accumulates into one stack local. Nothing is born on the heap, so nothing dies there.

This is exactly where N# tries to earn its keep. In ordinary code the allocation is still invisible; in a `[hot]` function, N#'s analyzer makes it *loud*. Any heap allocation on a hot path is flagged at build time as **NSYS010**, and the `alloc` keyword forces every real heap allocation to be spelled out in the source so it's greppable. A `stackalloc` buffer (a `Span<T>` that lives on the stack, no `unsafe` needed) sidesteps the heap entirely. The point isn't that N# is magic — it's that the silent tax becomes a visible, reviewable line item you opt into on purpose, instead of one your `.Select` hid from you.
keyTakeaways: Stack memory (locals, loop counters, spans) is free to allocate and auto-reclaimed on return; heap memory (`new` arrays/lists/closures) costs a GC tax later.
The classic hot-loop bug is a hidden allocation — LINQ chains and intermediate `List<T>`/arrays allocate iterators, closures, and backing buffers per call.
The fix is structural: fuse transform-then-reduce into one accumulating pass so no intermediate collection is ever born.
N# makes the tax visible — `[hot]` + NSYS010 flags any heap allocation at build time, and `alloc`/`stackalloc` force every heap site to be spelled out.

nsharp.note: `[hot]` + NSYS010 prove zero heap allocation at build time; the fused loop reads from a stack local and never builds an intermediate array.

csharp.note: The LINQ version is the readable trap: it allocates an iterator (and closure) per call. The hand-fused loop allocates nothing — and matches N# within ~1-5%.

rust.note: Borrows the slice (`&[i32]`) — no ownership transfer, no allocation; LLVM keeps `sum` in a register and may auto-vectorize the pass.

memoryStory: On these pure i32-array scalar kernels, N#, C#, and Rust all allocate **0 bytes on the heap** — everything lives in stack/registers, so the honest story is NOT "N# allocates less here." The story is the *cost model*: an idiomatic allocating version (C# `Select(...).Sum()`, or building a doubled array first) allocates an iterator/closure/backing array per call, whereas the N# `[hot]` fused loop is proven zero-alloc at build time by NSYS010. Any specific byte figure for the allocating version is illustrative unless measured with BenchmarkDotNet `--memory`; the measured fact is the 0-vs-nonzero allocation-site count, and on the checksum-sum kernel N# ties C# pre-SIMD (16.18 vs 16.22 ns at size 64; Apple M4, .NET 10, measured 2026-06) and beats the C# scalar baseline ~4.5x post-vectorization (222.5 vs 994.7 ns at 4096).

puzzle.prompt: Compute the sum of every value *doubled* — WITHOUT first building a doubled array. The naive approach builds an intermediate collection (an allocation per element); you must do it in a single `foreach` that accumulates into one running total (a stack local). Fill in the loop body of `SumDoubled` so the program prints the doubled-sum and the element count.
puzzle.successMessage: That's a fused transform-then-reduce: one pass, one stack local, zero heap allocations. The naive version would have allocated a whole doubled array just to throw it away — the exact hidden tax NSYS010 catches in a [hot] N# loop.
puzzle.hint: You don't need a second array. Inside the foreach, accumulate `number * 2` into `total` with `total = total + number * 2`. The sum of [3,1,4,1,5,2] is 16, and doubled that's 32.

title: Counting fast: predicates, masks, and the branch you avoid
subtitle: A per-element if is fine — until you teach a vector unit to count 8 lanes at once without ever branching.
concept:
Counting is the simplest interesting question you can ask of an array: "how many elements satisfy some condition?" Here the condition is a *range predicate* — is this integer a printable ASCII code, i.e. in `[32, 126]`? The obvious code walks the array, and for each element runs an `if`: if it's in range, bump a counter. That's correct, readable, and on a single value it's exactly what the machine should do.

The hidden cost shows up at scale, and it has a name: the **branch**. A modern CPU doesn't wait to find out which way an `if` goes — it *guesses*, runs ahead speculatively, and rewinds if it guessed wrong. When your data is predictable (all in range, or all out), the guess is nearly always right and the branch is almost free. When the data is a coin-flip mix, the predictor is wrong about half the time, and every misprediction costs a pipeline flush — tens of cycles thrown away, per element. Your tidy `if` quietly becomes the most expensive instruction in the loop.

The escape is to stop branching at all. A comparison like `x >= 32` doesn't *have* to drive a jump — it can produce a **mask**: a value that is `1` (or all-ones bits) when true and `0` when false. Counting then becomes pure arithmetic: `count += (x >= 32 && x <= 126) ? 1 : 0`, with no jump for the CPU to mispredict. This is **branchless** counting. It's the same answer, computed as a flat sequence of compares and adds the pipeline can chew through without ever guessing.

And once the count is branchless arithmetic, it's ready to go **wide**. A vector unit (SIMD) holds 8 or 16 integers in one register and does the same compare on all of them in a single instruction, producing 8–16 masks at once, which it adds into 8–16 running sub-counts in parallel. You sum the lanes at the very end. Same predicate, same total — but the work-per-instruction multiplied by the lane count. That is the leap the next module cashes in; this module is about seeing *why* the branch had to disappear first.
keyTakeaways: A range predicate `lo <= x <= hi` is just two compares — scalar, that's a per-element branch the CPU has to predict.
Mispredicted branches are the real tax: on coin-flip data each wrong guess flushes the pipeline (tens of cycles). Branchless turns the `if` into a mask you simply add.
Once counting is branchless arithmetic (compare -> 0/1 mask -> add), it vectorizes: 8-16 lanes compare and accumulate at once, lanes summed at the end.

Measured (Apple M4, .NET 10, BenchmarkDotNet, 2026-06): count-ascii at 4096 ints — N# now emits masked SIMD at 296.4ns vs C# scalar 1172.9ns = 4.0x faster than C#, closing the native gap from ~6.3x to ~1.6x. N# still trails Rust/C ~1.6x (RyuJIT-vs-LLVM codegen), not parity.

nsharp.note: [hot] guarantees no alloc/box/closure (NSYS clean); the range-predicate count auto-vectorizes to System.Numerics.Vector<int> — masked compares accumulated 8-16 lanes at a time, summed once at the end.

csharp.note: Idiomatic, correct, zero-alloc — but RyuJIT keeps it scalar with a per-element branch, so it lands at the ~1172.9ns/4096 baseline N# now beats 4.0x.

rust.note: The `as u32` on the boolean is the explicit branchless mask; LLVM packs the compares and accumulates across lanes, giving the ~183.9ns/4096 native floor (~1.6x ahead of N# today).

memoryStory: All three versions are pure i32-array scalar loops: zero heap allocations, everything in registers — measured identical on memory (2026-06), so the honest story here is NOT that N# allocates less. The memory lesson is the cost model: a naive high-level count like `data.Where(x => x >= 32 && x <= 126).Count()` materializes a per-element iterator/closure and can allocate per stage, whereas the N# `[hot]` span loop allocates ZERO and the NSYS010 analyzer *proves* it at build time. The number to remember is speed (4.0x over C#, measured), not bytes — the bytes are already zero on both sides.

puzzle.prompt: Count how many integers fall in the printable-ASCII range [32, 126] (inclusive). Walk the array with `foreach`, use an `if` with the two-sided range check, carry the count in a local, and print it as `Printable: <count>`. (No indexing, no `for`, no `while` — just `foreach` and an `if`.)
puzzle.successMessage: That's the count-ascii kernel. Notice the inner test is the whole game: `code >= 32 && code <= 126`. Written this way it's a two-sided range predicate the N# compiler turns into a branchless lane mask and accumulates 8-16 at a time — measured 4.0x faster than the C# scalar baseline at 4096 ints (M4, 2026-06).
puzzle.hint: The printable range is inclusive on both ends, so use `>=` and `<=`. Combine the two checks with `&&` inside a single `if`, and bump `count` by 1 when both hold. Of the ten codes — 10, 32, 65, 90, 126, 200, 13, 9, 100, 127 — exactly five land in [32, 126]: 32, 65, 90, 126, and 100 (note 127 is one past the top).

title: SIMD: doing many things in one instruction
subtitle: One core, one instruction, a whole row of lanes — and why a min/max scan is built for it
concept:
A normal CPU instruction does one thing: add these two numbers. SIMD — Single Instruction, Multiple Data — is the same silicon doing that one operation across a whole row of numbers at once. A SIMD vector register holds several values side by side, in "lanes," and one instruction operates on every lane simultaneously. How many lanes depends on the hardware: a 256-bit AVX2 register (x86) holds eight 32-bit integers, so one `add` adds eight pairs at once; a 128-bit NEON register (Apple M-series ARM, where this module's numbers were measured) holds four 32-bit integers, so it does four at once. Either way the core didn't get faster — it got *wider*. You feed it data in groups of lanes and it chews through each group in a single tick. One `min` instruction takes the smaller of every lane-pair simultaneously; one `max`, the larger.

Not every loop can use this. The magic only works when the order you process elements in doesn't matter. Summing an array is perfect: `(a+b)+c == a+(b+c)` (associative) and `a+b == b+a` (commutative), so you can split the array into N independent running totals — one per lane — add them all in parallel, and combine the partial sums at the very end. Same for finding the minimum and the maximum: `min` and `max` are associative *and* commutative over integers, so each lane can independently track "the smallest I've seen in my column," and you take the min across the lanes at the finish. Loops like these are called *embarrassingly vectorizable*.

Here's the catch that makes this module matter. In Rust and C, the LLVM compiler **automatically** spots these patterns and emits SIMD for you — that's a big chunk of why those languages crush a sum or a min/max loop. Stock .NET's JIT (RyuJIT) does **not** auto-vectorize them; it emits a plain scalar loop, one element per instruction. That's exactly why, before this work, N# (which ties C# on these kernels) was *10.5x behind native* on min-max-delta at 4096 elements — the single biggest gap of any kernel measured. The gap wasn't anything wrong with N#; it was scalar-vs-SIMD, RyuJIT-vs-LLVM.

So N#'s systems lane now does what RyuJIT won't: it recognizes the min/max reduction shape and **emits `System.Numerics.Vector<T>` directly**, lowering your `if a[i] < min` loop to lane-wise `Vector.Min` / `Vector.Max` (with four independent accumulators to hide latency, a horizontal fold, and a scalar tail). The width is whatever the running CPU's `Vector<int>.Count` is — four lanes on the M4 these numbers come from, eight on an AVX2 box. The win is real and measured (Apple M4, .NET 10, measured 2026-06): min-max-delta at 4096 elements went from 1535 ns (C# scalar) to **468 ns — 3.28x faster than C#**, closing that 10.5x native gap to about 3.2x. The remaining gap is the *two-pass* cost (min and max each re-scan the array); a fused single-pass is the planned follow-up.
keyTakeaways: SIMD = one instruction over many lanes: a 256-bit AVX2 register is eight int32s, a 128-bit NEON register (Apple M-series, where these numbers were measured) is four — processed in a single op either way. The core didn't speed up, it got wider.
A reduction is vectorizable only when order doesn't matter — sum, min, and max are associative+commutative, so each lane tracks its own running result and you combine across lanes at the end.
LLVM (Rust/C) auto-vectorizes these loops; stock .NET's RyuJIT does NOT — which is why N# was 10.5x behind native on min-max-delta at 4096 despite tying C#.

N#'s systems lane now emits System.Numerics.Vector<T> for min/max reductions: 468ns vs C#'s 1535ns at 4096 = 3.28x faster than C#, ~3.2x behind native (measured Apple M4, NEON 128-bit / 4 int32 lanes, 2026-06). The leftover gap is two-pass scanning; a fused single pass is next.

nsharp.note: You write the scalar fold; N# emits Vector.Min/Vector.Max so several int32 lanes fold in parallel (four on the measured M4) — 3.28x faster than the C# scalar baseline.

csharp.note: Clean and correct, but stock RyuJIT runs it one element at a time — this is the 1535ns/4096 scalar baseline N# now beats 3.28x.

rust.note: Same algorithm; LLVM emits packed SIMD min/max for free — the codegen N# now has to emit by hand because RyuJIT won't.

memoryStory: This kernel is a pure i32-array scalar fold, so it allocates ZERO bytes on the heap in N#, C#, and Rust alike — the speedup here is codegen (SIMD lanes), not memory. The honest memory story is the cost model: a naive high-level "max minus min" written with LINQ as `a.Max() - a.Min()` would walk the array twice through allocating enumerators, while the N# [hot] loop allocates nothing and the NSYS010 analyzer proves that zero at build time. (The 0-allocation claim is structural and certain; the LINQ-allocates contrast is illustrative, not from this benchmark.)

puzzle.prompt: Compute max-minus-min (the delta) over an array of integers using a single foreach that carries a running min and a running max. No indexing — seed both from a known starting value, then update each as you walk. Print the whole-number delta.
puzzle.successMessage: That's the min/max fold a real SIMD reduction runs in parallel — each lane carries its own min and max, then they fold to one at the end. Min is 9, max is 88, delta 79.
puzzle.hint: Inside the foreach, use two separate if-checks: if n < min then min = n, and if n > max then max = n. The max in [50,17,88,23,41,9,73] is 88 and the min is 9, so 88 - 9 = 79.

title: The Cost of Safety: Bounds Checks and How to Keep Them Free
subtitle: Why every array read in a safe language carries a tax — and the honest module where N# still trails native.
concept:
When you write `a[i]` in a memory-safe language, the CPU doesn't just go fetch the value. First it has to prove `i` is actually inside the array — `0 <= i < a.Length`. If it isn't, the program throws instead of reading some random neighboring memory. That proof is a *bounds check*: a compare and a conditional branch inserted before the load. This is the deal memory safety makes — you trade a tiny per-access cost for never reading or writing out of bounds. C does not make that deal, which is exactly why C programs have buffer-overflow bugs and N#, C#, and safe Rust mostly don't.

In a hot loop, "tiny per-access cost" adds up. If you walk a 4096-element array, that's 4096 compares-and-branches *on top of* the actual work, every single time the loop runs. The good news: the JIT is smart. For a clean *counted* loop — one where it can prove the index stays in range for the whole trip — RyuJIT (and LLVM, and every serious compiler) hoists the proof out and *elides* the per-iteration check entirely. The shape of your loop decides whether you pay the tax or not. A loop the compiler can reason about gets the check removed; a tangled one keeps paying.

But eliding bounds checks is only half the story, and this module is where we're going to be honest about the other half. Some loops have a shape the compiler can turn into SIMD — process several lanes at once with packed vector instructions. A plain sum or a range-count is that shape, and N# now auto-vectorizes those (it beats C# ~4x on them). Other loops carry a *dependency*: each iteration needs the result of the one before it. `count-transitions` is the poster child — to know if element *i* differs from element *i-1*, you have to have already looked at *i-1*. You can't process those lanes independently, so it stays scalar.

So here is the measured truth (Apple M4, .NET 10, measured 2026-06): on `count-transitions`, N# ties C# within ~0.25% (16.81 vs 16.85 ns at size 64; 1132 vs 1134 ns at 4096) — N# is as fast as the best the CLR has to offer. But it trails the best native (Rust/C) by **2.45x at size 64, widening to 4.54x at 4096**. That widening-with-size signature is the per-iteration indexed-load-plus-branch tax that LLVM schedules and unrolls more aggressively than RyuJIT does. Not everything vectorizes; here N# is CLR-fast but still behind LLVM, and now you know exactly why.
keyTakeaways: A bounds check is a compare-and-branch the compiler inserts before `a[i]` to prove the index is in range — the price of never reading out of bounds.
For clean counted loops the JIT *elides* the per-iteration check by proving the index in range once at loop entry; loop shape decides whether you keep paying.
`count-transitions` carries a dependency (each step needs the previous value), so it can't vectorize — it stays scalar in every language.

Honest result (measured 2026-06, Apple M4): N# ties C# within ~0.25% on count-transitions but trails the best native (Rust/C) 2.45x->4.54x as size grows. The gap is RyuJIT-vs-LLVM scalar codegen, not anything N#-specific.

nsharp.note: [hot] forbids alloc/box/closure; the clean counted loop lets RyuJIT elide the per-iteration bounds check — but the carried `previous` keeps it scalar, so it ties C# and trails LLVM.

csharp.note: The RyuJIT scalar baseline. Same counted-loop shape, same elided bounds check — N# matches it within ~0.25%.

rust.note: Safe indexing (bounds checks kept), but LLVM schedules/unrolls the scalar dependency chain tighter than RyuJIT — Rust is 2.34x faster than N# at size 64, widening to 4.54x at 4096 (best-native gap incl. C is 2.45x->4.54x). Measured Apple M4, 2026-06.

memoryStory: All three versions are pure i32-array scalar loops: zero heap allocations in N#, C#, and Rust alike — everything lives in registers and on the stack (measured 2026-06, Apple M4). So memory is NOT where they differ here. The honest memory story is the cost model: a naive high-level version (C# LINQ `.Zip(...).Count(x => ...)`, or building an intermediate `List<bool>` of comparisons) would allocate per element or per stage, while the `[hot]` counted loop allocates exactly zero — and N#'s NSYS010 analyzer *proves* that zero at build time. The allocation a naive version hides versus the zero the systems loop guarantees is the real memory lesson; this kernel's speed gap is pure codegen, not GC.

puzzle.prompt: Count the adjacent transitions in an array: how many times a value differs from the one right before it. The interpreter has no array indexing, so use `foreach` and carry the previous value across iterations (use a flag to skip the comparison on the very first element). The array is [3, 3, 7, 7, 7, 1, 1, 5] — print the transition count as a whole number.
puzzle.successMessage: Exactly 3 transitions (3->7, 7->1, 1->5). You carried `previous` across the foreach instead of indexing — which is the same carried dependency that keeps this kernel scalar in every language. That's why N# ties C# here but trails the best native (Rust/C) 2.45x-4.54x: not everything vectorizes, and we tell you why.
puzzle.hint: The transitions in [3, 3, 7, 7, 7, 1, 1, 5] are 3->7, 7->1, and 1->5 = 3. Guard the comparison with `first == 0` so the first element only seeds `previous`. Inside the loop, add 1 only when `first == 0 && value != previous`, then set `previous = value` and `first = 0` every iteration.

title: Latency vs throughput: when each step waits on the last
subtitle: The floor of what any compiler can do — and N# is already sitting on it.
concept:
Earlier modules vectorized loops by noticing the iterations were *independent*: summing an array, counting bytes in a range. Iteration 5 didn't need iteration 4's answer, so the CPU could run eight of them at once in a SIMD lane, or just keep several in flight on its many execution ports. That parallelism is what made the 4x wins possible.

A **rolling hash** breaks that. The loop body is `hash = ((hash * 31) + values[i]) & 65535` — every iteration *reads the hash that the previous iteration just wrote*. You cannot compute step 5 until step 4 finishes, because step 5's input literally is step 4's output. This is a **dependency chain** (also called a carried dependency): a single strand of work where each link waits on the one before it. There is nothing to spread across lanes, because there is only ever one live value of `hash`.

This is the difference between **throughput** and **latency**. Throughput is "how many independent multiplies can I retire per nanosecond" — and a modern core can do several at once. Latency is "how long does one multiply take from input to output, start to finish" — and you pay that *in full, in series*, once per iteration, because the next iteration is standing in line for the result. A dependency chain converts a throughput machine into a latency machine. The loop's speed is now `length × (latency of one multiply-add-mask)`, and no amount of SIMD, unrolling, or cleverness shrinks that — it's arithmetic.

So this is the floor. It's the one kernel where a compiler genuinely has almost nothing left to do, and it's exactly where N# is *closest* to native code: measured 1.44x behind Rust/C at 64 elements and 1.61x at 4096 (Apple M4, .NET 10, measured 2026-06). On the vectorizable kernels N# trailed native by up to 8.8x because RyuJIT left SIMD on the table — here there *is* no SIMD to leave on the table, so the only gap is small differences in how RyuJIT vs LLVM allocate registers and schedule the chain. N# ties C# to within ~5% here (tightest, ~0.03%, at n=4096; ~5% slower at n=64), and both sit right at the CLR floor.
keyTakeaways: A carried dependency — each iteration reads the previous iteration's output — serializes the loop: there is only one live accumulator, so there is nothing to run in parallel.
Latency-bound means the loop costs length × (latency of one operation), in series. SIMD, unrolling, and extra execution ports can't help because they need independent work to chew on.

This is the floor of what any compiler can do. Rolling-hash is the kernel where N# is closest to native: 1.44x (n=64) to 1.61x (n=4096) behind Rust/C, ties C# within ~5% — within ~0.03% at n=4096, ~5% at n=64 (Apple M4, measured 2026-06).

The residual ~1.5x gap to native here is pure RyuJIT-vs-LLVM register allocation and instruction scheduling on the chain — not anything N#-specific, and not something auto-vectorization could ever fix.

nsharp.note: [hot] proves zero alloc, but the vectorizer correctly leaves this scalar — the carried `hash` can't be split into lanes, so it stays one multiply-add-mask per step and tracks C# within ~5% (essentially identical at n=4096).

csharp.note: Identical scalar loop; RyuJIT emits one multiply-add-and per iteration. N# tracks this within ~5% (~0.03% apart at n=4096, ~5% at n=64) — both are at the CLR floor.

rust.note: LLVM faces the same carried chain and also can't vectorize it; its ~1.5x edge is tighter register allocation / scheduling on the dependency, not parallelism.

memoryStory: All three versions are a pure i32 scalar loop over an existing array: zero heap allocations in N#, C#, and Rust alike — everything lives in registers (measured: identical, 0 allocations). The honest memory contrast here is the cost model, not a measured delta: a naive high-level rolling hash that first did `values.Select(...).Aggregate(...)` would allocate per-stage intermediates, while the N# `[hot]` loop carries one `int` in a register and the NSYS010 analyzer proves zero allocation at build time. That illustrative LINQ allocation is the cost the systems loop guarantees away — it is not a number measured on this kernel.

puzzle.prompt: Compute a carried hash over a small array using the rule h = h*2 + x, one element at a time, with a foreach loop. Start the hash at 1. Each iteration must use the hash the previous iteration produced — that's the whole point: you can't parallelize it. Print the final hash. With the array below the answer is a small whole number.
puzzle.successMessage: That's the dependency chain in action: 1 -> 3 -> 6 -> 13 -> 27, each step waiting on the last. No SIMD lane could have run these in parallel, because every step's input is the previous step's output. This is exactly why rolling-hash is latency-bound — and exactly why it's the kernel where N# sits closest to native (~1.5x), tracks C# within ~5% (essentially identical at large arrays), and the vectorizer correctly leaves it alone.
puzzle.hint: Inside the foreach, reassign hash to its own new value: hash = hash * 2 + bit. Trace it by hand: 1 -> 1*2+1=3 -> 3*2+0=6 -> 6*2+1=13 -> 13*2+1=27.

title: Hidden costs: boxing and virtual dispatch
subtitle: Two ways a tidy-looking loop quietly allocates and refuses to inline — and how N# makes them visible.
concept:
A value type like `int` or a small `struct` normally lives in a CPU register or on the stack: free to create, free to copy, zero heap traffic. But the moment you put one into an `object` (or any interface variable), the runtime has to **box** it — allocate a little heap cell, copy the value in, and hand you a reference. Now you have a pointer chase, a future garbage-collection visit, and a copy back out (`unboxing`) every time you read it. One box is nanoseconds. A box *per element* in a hot loop is death by a thousand cuts: the loop that should touch only registers is instead minting garbage on every iteration.

**Virtual and interface dispatch** is the second hidden tax. When you call a method on a concrete type the JIT knows, it can jump straight there — and often **inline** the body, erasing the call entirely and letting later optimizations fold across it. When you call through an `interface` or `virtual` whose real type the JIT can't pin down (it can't *devirtualize*), it must instead read a method-table slot at runtime and make an **indirect jump**. That indirect call is slower on its own, but the real damage is that it's an optimization wall: the JIT can't inline through it, so it can't unroll, can't vectorize, can't const-fold across the boundary. The little call becomes a fence around everything fast.

These costs are invisible in most languages — the code reads fine, it just runs slow, and you only find out with a profiler. N#'s effect model surfaces them at *build time*. In a `[hot]` function, casting a value to `object` is flagged `NSYS020` ("boxing a value on a hot path"), and a call the JIT would have to dispatch at runtime is flagged `NSYS040` ("call uses runtime dispatch or an unsummarized interface-shaped API"). The fix the compiler suggests is the same one a perf engineer reaches for by hand: keep the receiver a **concrete type** and use **constrained generics** instead of interfaces, so dispatch stays direct and the value never leaves the stack.

So the discipline is simple to state: stay **monomorphic** (one concrete type the JIT can see) and **allocation-free** (no value ever wanders into an `object`). Do that, and a summing loop is just an `add` in a register, iteration after iteration — which is exactly what the puzzle below proves stays true even as the data flows through a foreach.
keyTakeaways: Boxing = a heap allocation + a copy every time a value type becomes an `object` or interface; per-element in a hot loop it turns a register add into GC traffic.
Un-devirtualizable interface/virtual calls cost an indirect jump AND block inlining — which blocks unrolling, vectorization, and const-folding across the call.
N# flags these at build time: `NSYS020` for boxing, `NSYS040` for runtime dispatch in `[hot]` code — no profiler needed to find them.
The cure is concrete types + constrained generics (and `[hot]` to enforce it): dispatch stays direct, the value never leaves the stack, allocation stays at zero.

nsharp.note: [hot] turns boxing (NSYS020) and undevirtualized dispatch (NSYS040) into build errors, so the loop is provably register-only.

csharp.note: Both compile clean in C#; only the concrete version is allocation-free, and nothing tells you which is which.

rust.note: Rust defaults to monomorphized, stack-resident values; heap boxing (Box/dyn) is explicit, never accidental.

memoryStory: On this exact kernel all three languages allocate zero — a concrete `int` sum is registers everywhere, so there is no measured allocation difference to claim. The honest memory story is the cost *model*: the boxed C# variant above performs one heap allocation per element (illustrative, not a measured ns row), and idiomatic high-level code that funnels values through `object`/interfaces or builds intermediate `List<T>` stages hides exactly that per-element traffic — whereas the N# `[hot]` loop is guaranteed allocation-free, and NSYS020/NSYS040 prove it at build time instead of leaving it for a profiler.

puzzle.prompt: Write a monomorphic, allocation-free sum. Complete `SumValues` so it adds every number in the array using a plain `int` accumulator (no boxing, no `object`) and prints the total. Keep it concrete — the whole point is that the value never leaves a register.
puzzle.successMessage: That loop is pure register arithmetic — no box, no heap, no dispatch. In Systems N# it would clear [hot] with NSYS020 and NSYS040 both silent.
puzzle.hint: You already have an int accumulator `total` and an int `n` each iteration. Add them directly: `total = total + n`. Don't introduce an `object` — that's the boxing trap the lesson is about.

title: The systems lane: cost becomes a contract
subtitle: Everything you've learned, enforced by the compiler — and explained when you break it.
concept:
Across this course you kept arriving at the same destination by hand: one tight pass over the data, no heap allocation, no boxing, no per-element bounds tax, and — where the shape allows — SIMD. Each time, *you* were the one holding the line. You read the loop, reasoned about what it allocated, and trusted yourself not to slip a `.Where(...).Select(...)` or a hidden closure into the hot path. That works until it doesn't: a refactor three weeks later quietly reintroduces an allocation and nobody notices until production.

N#'s systems lane turns that discipline into a *contract the compiler enforces*. You mark a function `[hot]` and you've made a promise: this is steady-state code, so no heap allocation, no boxing, no closure or delegate construction, no virtual dispatch, no throwing. The analyzer holds you to it. The moment the hot path violates the cost model, you get a specific diagnostic from the `NSYS` family — `NSYS010` for an allocation, `NSYS020` for boxing, `NSYS030` for a closure, `NSYS040` for a virtual call — naming exactly what cost slipped in and, if it's hiding behind a callee, the full call chain that leads to it. Cost stops being invisible. It becomes a thing you can see, check in CI, and explain in plain language.

This is what the whole lane is built from. `Result<T,E>` is a `readonly struct`, so structured errors cost zero allocations on the success path — no exceptions on the happy road. `alloc` makes every heap allocation a word you say out loud and can grep for; `stackalloc` hands you a `Span<T>` on the stack with no `unsafe` block, its lifetime checked so it can't escape its frame. `ref struct` + spans give zero-copy parsing with compile-time lifetime checking. And the auto-vectorizer recognizes the exact reduction and range-count shapes you've been writing and emits `System.Numerics.Vector<T>` directly — the part that makes systems N# *fast*, not just *checked*.

The honest promise is precise: not "faster than Rust." It's "CLR costs visible, checkable, explainable." Measured on an Apple M4 (2026-06), N# ties C# within ~1–5% everywhere, and after the SIMD work it *beats* the C# scalar baseline 3.3–4.5x on the vectorizable kernels. It still trails native (Rust/C) by ~1.4x on latency-bound code up to ~3.2x post-vectorization — and that gap is RyuJIT-vs-LLVM codegen, nothing N#-specific. The systems lane's job isn't to win a drag race against LLVM. It's to make sure the cost you *think* you're paying is the cost you're actually paying, and to tell you the instant that stops being true.
keyTakeaways: `[hot]` is a promise the compiler enforces: no alloc, boxing, closures, virtual dispatch, or throws in steady-state code. The `NSYS` family names each violation in plain language — `NSYS010` alloc, `NSYS020` boxing, `NSYS030` closure, `NSYS040` virtual dispatch — and follows the call chain so cost can't hide behind a callee.

The pieces fit together: `Result<T,E>` (zero-alloc errors), `alloc`/`stackalloc` (allocation you say out loud, stack spans with no `unsafe`), `ref struct` + lifetime checks, and auto-vectorization of reduction/range-count loops. The full surface is Path A — the Systems Tour.

Honest telemetry (Apple M4, measured 2026-06): N# ties C# within ~1–5% everywhere and beats the C# scalar baseline 3.3–4.5x on vectorizable kernels post-SIMD. It still trails Rust/C by ~1.4x (latency-bound) to ~3.2x (min-max post-SIMD) — a RyuJIT-vs-LLVM codegen gap, not anything N#-specific.

The memory win on these scalar i32 kernels is identical across N#/C#/Rust (zero heap). The real difference is the cost *model*: a naive `.Where().Select().Count()` allocates per element/stage and hides it; the `[hot]` span loop allocates zero and `NSYS010` proves it at build time.

The promise is 'CLR costs visible, checkable, explainable,' not 'faster than Rust.' That confidence is the point: you don't have to trust yourself to keep the hot path clean — the compiler does it for you.

nsharp.note: [hot] enforces zero-cost steady state; the reduction shape auto-vectorizes to Vector<int> — 4.5x faster than the C# scalar baseline at 4096 (M4, 2026-06).

csharp.note: Identical algorithm; N# ties this within ~1-5% pre-SIMD. RyuJIT emits scalar code here, so the SIMD gap is what N#'s vectorizer closes.

rust.note: LLVM emits SIMD+unrolled code, so native runs ~2x faster than N# even post-vectorization at 4096 — the residual is RyuJIT-vs-LLVM, not N#-specific.

memoryStory: On these pure i32-array loops the heap allocation is identical across N#, C#, and Rust: zero — it's all stack and registers, so there's no memory delta to claim here (measured). The real story is the cost *model*: an idiomatic high-level version (C# `.Where(...).Select(...).Count()`, or building an intermediate `List<T>`) allocates per element or per stage and hides it, whereas the `[hot]` span loop allocates zero and `NSYS010` proves that at build time. That per-stage allocation figure is illustrative of the naive pattern, not a measured number from this kernel.

puzzle.prompt:
Capstone: one tight pass, zero allocation. Over a single array, in ONE foreach, do two jobs at once — accumulate the total sum of every item, AND count how many items fall in the inclusive range 5..15. Then print both whole numbers on two lines, exactly:

Sum: 59
In range: 4

This is the systems-lane mindset in miniature: carry both accumulators across one loop instead of making two passes (or, worse, allocating an intermediate filtered collection).
puzzle.successMessage: That's the systems lane in one loop: two accumulators, one pass, zero allocation. In real N# you'd mark this [hot] — and the compiler would PROVE there's no hidden alloc, boxing, or closure, and even vectorize the sum. You've got the mental model; Path A (the Systems Tour) has the full surface.
puzzle.hint: You already have the running sum. Add a single `if` inside the same foreach: when `n >= 5 && n <= 15`, bump `inRange` by 1. No second loop, no array indexing — just carry both totals across the one pass. 10, 7, 5, and 14 are in range; 3 and 20 are not.
